session: Session 3 - Non-verbal communication and the 93% myth
bullets: Claim '93% of communication is non-verbal' comes from a 1967 Mehrabian study on 167 college students about message incongruence (words and non-verbal behaviour not matching).
The statistic is widely considered a myth (source cited: Novak, 2020).
Non-verbal communication still has real impact: complementarity, synchrony, regulation.
Warm-up activities: Charades (45 seconds, no sound, no mouthing; exaggerate body language) and 'Just a minute' (speak 1 minute non-stop).
Charades categories: presentation and speaker tropes, workplace/virtual mishaps, expressive-performance jobs.
examTip: Know why the 93% figure is misleading (only incongruent messages). Common mistake: quoting 93% as a general rule.

session: Rhetoric: Logos, Pathos, Ethos and Persuasive Devices
bullets: Three appeals: Logos (logic, reason), Pathos (emotions), Ethos (credibility, trustworthiness).
Devices from Simon Lancaster 'Speak like a Leader': three breathless sentences, three repetitive sentences, three balancing statements.
Metaphor: imagery increases emotional appeal. Exaggeration: amplifies emotion. Rhyme: signals truth, memorable.
Also listed: the 3's effect, repetition, balance, rhetorical question.
Good speeches have a central message and a call to action.
Example text: 'I have a dream' by Martin Luther King Jr (repetition, metaphor, call to action).
examTip: Be ready to identify appeals and devices in a speech excerpt. Common mistake: naming a device without explaining why it works.

bullets: Pitch variety and intonation: vary your tone within sentences.
Emphasise key words: stress changes the meaning ('I never said she stole my money' shifts with each stressed word).
Articulation: use tongue twisters (Peter Piper, seashells) and vowel/consonant practice.
Find your pace: speaking too quickly hurts clarity.
Dramatic vs dull opening: 'Floods. Plagues. Famine. Death.' beats the earnest 'today I will speak to you about global warming'.
Pro tip: leave out or replace hard-to-pronounce words in your speech.
examTip: Practical delivery points are likely. Common mistake: flat, rushed delivery with an announcement-style opening.

session: Hooks, Openings and Case Presentation Structure (Fact Deck)
bullets: Use a HOOK: story, joke, famous quote, film/series reference, proverb, shocking fact or statistic, poem or song, question, object or demo, verbal picture.
Fact deck structure: Who was involved (parties, photos/logos, necessary facts).
What happened: brief, accurate description; which laws were broken (define them); how each party was involved.
Where and Why: location and motives; who gained what.
When: timeline by month and year. How: how it unfolded, how they were caught, who brought them to justice.
Aftermath: charges, jail time, fines, future of the company and persons. End with Sources.
examTip: Cover all of who / what / where / why / when / how / aftermath in order. Common mistake: wrong or vague facts and font smaller than allowed.
